script.opening: "Hi. I've just registered with you after moving, and I'm honestly really anxious about this call. I'm a trans woman, I've been on hormones for three years, but my supply's about to run out and the gender clinic waiting list is years long. I've had GPs basically refuse to help before, like it's not their problem. I just… I can't go back to how I felt before I started. Please — can you help me not crash?"

facts.text: If asked: oestradiol gel, two pumps a day, and cyproterone 12.5 mg a day, started three years ago by a private gender clinic. You last had blood tests six months ago and "they were fine". You have about a week left.

You lost your job when you moved and can no longer afford the private clinic, which discharged you. You were referred to an NHS gender identity clinic two years ago — still waiting, letter on your phone.
No clots, no migraine with aura, no liver problems, non-smoker, BMI normal. Blood pressure normal last time. No allergies. No other medicines.
"I've looked at buying online. People do it. I don't want to, but I will if I have to."

Before hormones you were very depressed and took an overdose at 21. Since starting hormones: "I feel like me." Now, with them running out: low, sleeping badly, and "I've had the thought that I'd rather not be here than go back to that." No plan, no stockpiled tablets, no recent self-harm. Your best friend lives nearby and you would tell her.
26, works in a café, lives in a flat share. Name on your record is Robyn; you use she/her.

Nervous, braced for rejection. If the doctor uses your name and pronouns naturally and is warm, you relax. If they say "this isn't something GPs do" and stop, become quietly hopeless: "So I'm on my own, then." If they are honest that they need to get specialist advice and promise to try to find a safe way to bridge, ask about your suicidal thoughts properly and agree a plan for this week, you are hugely relieved.

ice.ideas: "If my hormones stop, I'll crash back to how I was."
ice.concerns: Being refused again; and (only if asked) thoughts that you would rather not be here.
ice.expectations: "Can you help me not run out?" You understand the doctor may need to get advice first, as long as they genuinely try.

"I can't go back to how I felt before." — say in the opening.
"People buy them online, you know." — say if the doctor hesitates about prescribing.

checkpoints.text: Treats the patient with RESPECT and affirmation from the outset (correct name and pronouns, no othering/curiosity), recognising the fear of rejection — and does NOT refuse to engage on "not my area of expertise" grounds while leaving her without treatment

Assesses MENTAL-HEALTH RISK explicitly: the distress and the hint of suicidal thoughts at the prospect of stopping hormones — ideation, plan, intent, protective factors — recognising this as a safety issue, not merely administrative

Understands and considers a BRIDGING PRESCRIPTION as harm reduction: continuing her established hormone regimen to prevent abrupt cessation (and unregulated self-medication) while awaiting specialist review — an option the GMC says a GP may consider (not an obligation) when the patient is self-medicating or highly likely to and it reduces the risk of self-harm, with gender-specialist advice and the lowest acceptable dose — while being honest about the RCGP’s (2024) more cautious position — rather than leaving a gap without discussion

Arranges it SAFELY: baseline checks/monitoring as appropriate, seeks advice from a gender specialist/endocrinologist (shared care where possible), and ensures the GIC referral is in place and chases the wait — not bridging in a vacuum
Addresses the risk of UNREGULATED self-sourced hormones (unsafe/unmonitored) as a key reason bridging is harm-reductive, and provides safety/monitoring advice
Meets her with warmth and dignity FIRST, validating the exhaustion of having to justify herself and the previous poor experiences, so she feels safe rather than judged
Responds to the suicidal ideation with compassion and a safety plan, treating her whole wellbeing — not just the prescription

Safety-nets and follows up: the bridging prescription and monitoring plan, specialist advice/shared care, GIC referral chased, crisis routes if suicidal thoughts escalate (urgent/111/crisis team/A&E), trans-inclusive support resources, and a follow-up — ensuring she is safe and supported, not left to crash

worked.txt: "Robyn, first — thank you for trusting me with this, and I’m sorry you’ve been let down before; that shouldn’t have happened. I want to help, and I’m not going to leave you to run out. Let’s sort this together. Have I got your name right, and can I check the pronouns you’d like me to use?"

"Can I ask something important, gently — you said you can’t go back to how you felt before. When you think about the hormones stopping, do you ever have thoughts of not wanting to be here, or of harming yourself? … Thank you for being honest. That matters to me as much as the prescription, and I’ll make sure you’re supported, not just medicated."

"Here’s what I can do: the doctors’ regulator, the GMC, says a GP may consider what’s called a bridging prescription — continuing your established hormones — for someone in your situation, so you don’t suddenly stop and aren’t forced to buy them unregulated online, which is genuinely unsafe. It isn’t automatic: I need advice from a gender specialist first, and I’d use the lowest dose that works for you. I’m treating this as keeping you safe while the specialist service catches up."

"I’ll do it safely — a few baseline blood tests and blood-pressure check, and I’ll get advice from a gender specialist or hormone doctor so I’m prescribing the right doses for you, ideally as shared care. I’ll also check your gender-clinic referral is active and chase where I can, because that wait is far too long."

"I want to be honest about why I’m doing this: leaving you without your hormones risks your mental health and pushes people towards buying them from unsafe sources. Bridging you is the safer, kinder option, and it’s the right thing to do while you wait."

"So: I’ll get a gender specialist’s advice straight away so I can arrange the bridging prescription safely, do the baseline checks, and chase your referral. If those darker thoughts get stronger before I see you, here are the crisis numbers and that’s a 999/A&E matter if you ever feel unsafe. I’ll point you to some good trans-inclusive support too. You came in braced to fight for basic care — you don’t have to fight me. I’ve got you."

f.learning: A trans patient established on hormones whose supply is running out, facing a years-long gender-clinic wait, is a situation in which a BRIDGING prescription should be actively considered as harm reduction — not a reflex refusal. GMC guidance says a GP may consider — it is not an obligation — a bridging prescription to continue established hormones where the patient is self-medicating with unregulated hormones or highly likely to, to reduce the risk of self-harm or suicide, with gender-specialist advice and the lowest acceptable dose (the RCGP’s 2024 position statement is more cautious and does not see initiating hormones as a core GP role without additional expertise); it aims to prevent the harms of abrupt cessation and of patients resorting to unregulated self-sourced hormones, ideally with gender-specialist/endocrinology advice and shared care, plus baseline monitoring, while the specialist referral is in place and chased. Crucially, abrupt cessation risks a mental-health crisis: the hint of suicidal ideation at the prospect of stopping/detransitioning must be assessed and safety-planned — this is a safety issue, not an administrative one. The examinable hidden agenda is fear of rejection and the exhaustion of having to justify herself after previous poor experiences; meet her with respect and affirmation FIRST (correct name/pronouns, no othering), assess and support her whole wellbeing, do not refuse on "not my expertise" grounds while leaving her without treatment, and safety-net with crisis routes and trans-inclusive support. Abruptly stopping established hormones causes significant distress, may precipitate or worsen mental-health crisis (including suicidality), and frequently drives patients to UNREGULATED self-sourced hormones (unsafe, unmonitored). The hint of suicidal thoughts must be assessed — this is a safety issue, not just an administrative one.

knowledge.guideline: GMC ethical guidance — Trans healthcare (bridging prescriptions) · RCGP position statement on the GP’s role in transgender care (2024) · NICE NG225 — Self-harm (2022)
knowledge.summary: A GP may, but is not obliged to, issue a bridging prescription to someone established on hormones who is at risk of self-sourcing or of self-harm, after seeking gender-specialist advice and at the lowest acceptable dose. Robyn’s hint of suicidal thoughts makes this a safety consultation as well as a prescribing one.

points.t: GMC guidance: a GP may consider a bridging prescription where a patient is already self-medicating with unregulated hormones, or is highly likely to, and it is intended to reduce the risk of self-harm or suicide. Seek gender-specialist advice and prescribe the lowest acceptable dose. It is harm reduction, not starting treatment.

The RCGP (2024) does not see initiating hormones as part of the core GP role without extended expertise. Robyn is not asking for initiation — she is established on treatment. Explain openly what you can and cannot do, and do not hide behind “not my area”.

Ask directly about thoughts, plans, intent, previous self-harm and what keeps her safe. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or scales to predict suicide or allocate care; assess needs and make a safety plan with the person.

Confirm the current regimen from evidence (previous prescriptions or clinic letters). Baseline blood pressure, weight, smoking status and bloods as advised by the specialist (typically hormone levels, liver function, lipids, prolactin, and U&E if the anti-androgen is spironolactone). Oestrogen raises VTE risk; transdermal routes carry less risk than oral (BNF).

Confirm the NHS adult gender service referral is active (in England the single national waiting list is managed by the Gender National Referral Support Service from October 2026) and record the date; seek advice from a gender specialist or endocrinologist and aim for a shared-care arrangement. Keep monitoring whether or not you prescribe.
Use her name and pronouns and update the record. Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010. Offer screening by anatomy rather than recorded gender.

model.text: Hello, is that Robyn Achebe? It’s Dr Lee — welcome to the practice. Can I check your date of birth, and that you’re somewhere private? And which pronouns would you like me to use?
model.why: Identity and privacy checks; asks pronouns naturally

model.text: She and her. And yes, I’m on my own. I’m honestly really anxious about this call. I’m a trans woman, I’ve been on hormones three years, my supply runs out in a week, and the clinic waiting list is years long. I’ve had GPs refuse before like it’s not their problem.
Thank you for telling me, Robyn, and I’m sorry you’ve had that experience. I want to help you, and I’ll be honest with you about how. Can we go through things together?
model.why: Acknowledges past rejection and commits to honesty

model.text: Yes. Thank you. I didn’t expect that.
Tell me about your treatment so far — what you take, how, and who has been prescribing it.
model.why: Establishes the regimen and its source

model.text: Oestradiol and an anti-androgen. I started through a specialist service, then went private. That’s fallen through now. I should be able to find the old prescriptions and letters.

That’s really useful — could you send copies of those letters and prescriptions to the practice? I’ll need them to confirm the exact doses. And have you had any blood tests or blood-pressure checks recently?
model.why: Seeks evidence of the regimen and monitoring history

model.text: I’ll look them out and send them today. Bloods — not for a while.
Okay. Do you smoke, and have you or your family ever had a clot in the leg or lung?
model.why: Screens VTE risk relevant to oestrogen

model.text: No smoking, no clots that I know of.
You said you can’t go back to how you felt before. Can you tell me what you mean?
model.why: Follows the emotional cue with an open question

model.text: Before hormones I was in a really dark place. The thought of it stopping… I don’t know if I could do it again.
Thank you for trusting me with that. I need to ask directly, because it matters as much as the prescription: have you had thoughts of ending your life, or of harming yourself?
Sometimes. When I think about running out. I haven’t made any plans. I just don’t want to feel like that again.
I’m glad you told me. Have you ever acted on thoughts like that, and what helps keep you safe when they come?
model.why: Explores history, intent and protective factors

model.text: No, never acted on them. The hormones help. And knowing someone is actually helping.
And if the prescription didn’t happen, what would you do?
Honestly? I’d probably buy them online. I know that’s risky.

Thank you for being honest. Here’s where I stand. The GMC’s guidance allows a GP to give what’s called a bridging prescription — continuing hormones you’re already established on — when stopping would put you at risk, including buying them unregulated or your mental health. I’d do that with advice from a gender specialist, at the right dose, with monitoring. I can’t start new treatments or change your regimen myself, but I can help you avoid a gap.
model.why: Explains the GMC bridging criteria honestly, including limits

model.text: So you’ll actually do it?

I’m going to work to make it happen before you run out. The one thing I need is the confirmed doses from your letters and a quick specialist check. Buying online would mean unknown doses and no monitoring, and that’s exactly what I want to avoid.
model.why: Commits to a timely plan and names the harm-reduction rationale

model.text: That’s more than I hoped for.

Here’s the plan. Send the letters today. I’ll contact a gender specialist for advice this week. I’d like you to come in for a blood-pressure check and bloods. I’ll also confirm your clinic referral is active and note the date, and update your record with your name and pronouns. Does that work?
model.why: Concrete plan with monitoring, specialist advice, referral check and records

model.text: Yes. That’s brilliant.

Now, let’s make a plan for those darker thoughts. If they get stronger or you start to feel unsafe, call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, contact Samaritans on 116 123 any time, or call 999 or go to A&E if you’re in immediate danger. Is there someone you can talk to if things feel hard?
model.why: Safety plan with specific crisis routes

model.text: There are people I can talk to. I’ll reach out.
Good. I’ll ring you in two or three days with an update, well before you run out. Could you tell me what you’re doing next, so I know I’ve been clear?
Send my letters, book bloods and a blood-pressure check, don’t buy online, and ring 111 or Samaritans if I feel unsafe. You’ll call me in a few days.
That’s it. You came in expecting to have to fight for this — you don’t have to fight me. Anything else before we finish?
model.why: Reflects her hidden fear and shares the floor

model.text: No. Thank you. I can breathe again.

social.t: Trans people often meet discrimination in healthcare and face very long waits for gender services, which drives distress, disengagement and self-sourcing.
Private prescribing and monitoring are costly; when funding ends, people are pushed to unregulated online supply.

legal.t: Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic. Refusing care or treating her less favourably because she is trans may be unlawful discrimination.
Update her name and title on request. If she holds a Gender Recognition Certificate, information about her gender history is protected (Gender Recognition Act 2004, s22).

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): personal beliefs must not affect care. GMC trans healthcare guidance sets out when bridging may be considered and expects specialist advice and monitoring.
The prescriber takes responsibility. Confirm the regimen, seek specialist advice, document the rationale and risk discussion, and agree shared care where possible.

community.t: Samaritans (116 123), NHS 111 mental health option, LGBT+ helplines such as Switchboard, and local trans peer-support groups.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with a plan, intent or previous attempts — same-day mental health assessment
Plans to self-source unregulated hormones — unknown doses, no monitoring
Personal or family history of VTE, smoking, or high BP — affects oestrogen safety
psychosocial: Past rejection by GPs and exhaustion at having to justify herself
Her support network — who she can talk to
ice: Idea: she needs a bridging prescription to avoid running out
Concern: being refused again, “crashing”, and the return of suicidal thoughts
Expectation: help and to be treated with respect

playbook.diagnosis: “You’re established on hormones, the supply is about to stop, and stopping would put your mental health and your safety at risk. That is exactly the situation GMC guidance on bridging prescriptions is meant for.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A bridging prescription is like a temporary bridge over a gap in the road — it keeps you moving safely until the specialist service can take over again.”

management.reflectIce: “You expected another refusal and you’re frightened of going back to how you felt before. I’m not going to leave you with a gap.”
management.psychosocial: Affirm her identity, update the record, encourage her to use her own support network, and offer ongoing mental health support alongside the prescription.
sharedPlan: Obtain evidence of the current regimen; gender-specialist advice this week; bridging prescription at the lowest acceptable dose (GMC)
Baseline BP, weight and bloods as advised; VTE risk review; aim for shared care
Confirm the GIC referral and date; name and pronouns updated; anatomy-based screening
safetyNet: Crisis routes: NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans 116 123, 999 or A&E if in immediate danger
Call-back within 2–3 days, before the supply runs out; ongoing review

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating it as a prescribing question alone. The marks sit in respect, a direct suicide question, and an honest, workable bridging plan.

items.fail: Refusing because “hormones are specialist-only” and signposting the waiting list.
items.why: GMC guidance allows bridging in exactly this situation. A refusal leaves her at risk of self-harm and self-sourcing.
items.fix: Explain the GMC position, seek specialist advice, and commit to a timeline before the supply ends.

items.fail: Prescribing whatever she says she takes, with no evidence, advice or monitoring.
items.why: The GMC expects specialist advice, the lowest acceptable dose and monitoring.
items.fix: Get the letters, check BP and bloods, seek advice, and document the rationale.

items.why: “I can’t go back to how I felt before” is a cue. Missing it is unsafe.
items.fix: Ask directly about thoughts, plans and history, and co-produce a safety plan (NICE NG225).

items.fail: Misgendering or asking intrusive questions about her identity.
items.why: It repeats the rejection she expected and breaks trust.
items.fix: Ask pronouns early, use her name, and keep questions relevant to her treatment.

items.fail: Hiding behind policy — “it’s not my area”.
items.why: Examiners mark down defensive practice that puts the doctor’s comfort before the patient’s safety.
items.fix: Be honest about your limits and what you will do anyway.

items.why: Her supply ends in a week; a deadline needs a date.
items.fix: “I’ll ring you in two or three days, well before you run out.”

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name 111 mental health option, Samaritans 116 123 and 999/A&E.

wordPics.fail: Refuses on “not my expertise” and signposts the waiting list; misgenders her; never asks about suicidal thoughts; or prescribes unknown doses with no advice or monitoring.
wordPics.pass: Respectful; asks about suicidal thoughts; knows GMC bridging guidance; plans specialist advice and monitoring; checks the referral; gives crisis numbers.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains both the GMC position and the limits of the GP role transparently; explores self-sourcing and names it as the harm being reduced; gets the regimen evidenced; commits to a timeline before the supply runs out; safety plan co-produced; she ends the call feeling respected rather than processed.

avoid.dont: “I’m afraid hormones aren’t something GPs can prescribe — you’ll have to wait for the clinic.”
avoid.instead: “The GMC’s guidance allows a bridging prescription in situations like yours — let’s work out how to do it safely.”
avoid.why: A flat refusal ignores GMC guidance and leaves her at risk of self-harm and self-sourcing.

avoid.dont: “So when did you decide you were trans?”
avoid.instead: “Tell me about your treatment so far.”
avoid.why: Intrusive curiosity about identity is othering and irrelevant to the task.

avoid.dont: “You’re not going to do anything silly, are you?”
avoid.instead: “Have you had thoughts of ending your life, or of harming yourself?”
avoid.why: A leading question invites a “no”; a direct question gets the truth.

Anti-androgen — previously prescribed privately, not yet on practice repeat
SCA_STEM.recent: New registration. NHS gender identity clinic referral in place with a long wait. Private hormone supply has ended.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: hormones run out in a week — asking for a bridging prescription.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: GMC ethical guidance — Trans healthcare (bridging prescriptions) · RCGP position statement on the GP’s role in transgender care (2024) · NICE NG225 — Self-harm (2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A GP may, but is not obliged to, issue a bridging prescription to someone established on hormones who is at risk of self-sourcing or of self-harm, after seeking gender-specialist advice and at the lowest acceptable dose. Robyn’s hint of suicidal thoughts makes this a safety consultation as well as a prescribing one.

points.t: GMC guidance: a GP may consider a bridging prescription where a patient is already self-medicating with unregulated hormones, or is highly likely to, and it is intended to reduce the risk of self-harm or suicide. Seek gender-specialist advice and prescribe the lowest acceptable dose. It is harm reduction, not starting treatment.

The RCGP (2024) does not see initiating hormones as part of the core GP role without extended expertise. Robyn is not asking for initiation — she is established on treatment. Explain openly what you can and cannot do, and do not hide behind “not my area”.

Ask directly about thoughts, plans, intent, previous self-harm and what keeps her safe. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or scales to predict suicide or allocate care; assess needs and make a safety plan with the person.

Confirm the current regimen from evidence (previous prescriptions or clinic letters). Baseline blood pressure, weight, smoking status and bloods as advised by the specialist (typically hormone levels, liver function, lipids, prolactin, and U&E if the anti-androgen is spironolactone). Oestrogen raises VTE risk; transdermal routes carry less risk than oral (BNF).

Confirm the NHS adult gender service referral is active (in England the single national waiting list is managed by the Gender National Referral Support Service from October 2026) and record the date; seek advice from a gender specialist or endocrinologist and aim for a shared-care arrangement. Keep monitoring whether or not you prescribe.
Use her name and pronouns and update the record. Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010. Offer screening by anatomy rather than recorded gender.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked identity and privacy; asked pronouns; let her explain the situation and her previous experiences.
Move to a new area, loss of private supply, years-long wait, support network.
Followed “I can’t go back to how I felt before” into a direct suicide question.
Idea (needs a bridging script); concern (refusal again, crashing, suicidal thoughts); expectation (help and respect).
BP, weight, VTE risk, baseline bloods as advised by the specialist; evidence of current regimen.
Risk from abrupt cessation, self-sourcing, depression or suicidality, oestrogen-related VTE risk.
Suicide risk explored (thoughts, plans, history, protective factors) without relying on a risk score (NICE NG225).
Established hormone treatment at risk of interruption, with suicidal ideation and self-sourcing risk — meets GMC bridging criteria.
Bridging prescription after specialist advice at the lowest acceptable dose; monitoring; shared care aim; GIC referral confirmed.
Mental health support and safety plan; record updated with name and pronouns; anatomy-based screening.
Call-back within days, before supply runs out; 111 mental health option, Samaritans, 999/A&E.

social.t: Trans people often meet discrimination in healthcare and face very long waits for gender services, which drives distress, disengagement and self-sourcing.
Private prescribing and monitoring are costly; when funding ends, people are pushed to unregulated online supply.

legal.t: Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic. Refusing care or treating her less favourably because she is trans may be unlawful discrimination.
Update her name and title on request. If she holds a Gender Recognition Certificate, information about her gender history is protected (Gender Recognition Act 2004, s22).

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): personal beliefs must not affect care. GMC trans healthcare guidance sets out when bridging may be considered and expects specialist advice and monitoring.
The prescriber takes responsibility. Confirm the regimen, seek specialist advice, document the rationale and risk discussion, and agree shared care where possible.

community.t: Samaritans (116 123), NHS 111 mental health option, LGBT+ helplines such as Switchboard, and local trans peer-support groups.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with a plan, intent or previous attempts — same-day mental health assessment
Plans to self-source unregulated hormones — unknown doses, no monitoring
Personal or family history of VTE, smoking, or high BP — affects oestrogen safety
psychosocial: Past rejection by GPs and exhaustion at having to justify herself
Her support network — who she can talk to
ice: Idea: she needs a bridging prescription to avoid running out
Concern: being refused again, “crashing”, and the return of suicidal thoughts
Expectation: help and to be treated with respect

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’re established on hormones, the supply is about to stop, and stopping would put your mental health and your safety at risk. That is exactly the situation GMC guidance on bridging prescriptions is meant for.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A bridging prescription is like a temporary bridge over a gap in the road — it keeps you moving safely until the specialist service can take over again.”

management.reflectIce: “You expected another refusal and you’re frightened of going back to how you felt before. I’m not going to leave you with a gap.”
management.psychosocial: Affirm her identity, update the record, encourage her to use her own support network, and offer ongoing mental health support alongside the prescription.
sharedPlan: Obtain evidence of the current regimen; gender-specialist advice this week; bridging prescription at the lowest acceptable dose (GMC)
Baseline BP, weight and bloods as advised; VTE risk review; aim for shared care
Confirm the GIC referral and date; name and pronouns updated; anatomy-based screening
safetyNet: Crisis routes: NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans 116 123, 999 or A&E if in immediate danger
Call-back within 2–3 days, before the supply runs out; ongoing review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating it as a prescribing question alone. The marks sit in respect, a direct suicide question, and an honest, workable bridging plan.

items.fail: Refusing because “hormones are specialist-only” and signposting the waiting list.
items.why: GMC guidance allows bridging in exactly this situation. A refusal leaves her at risk of self-harm and self-sourcing.
items.fix: Explain the GMC position, seek specialist advice, and commit to a timeline before the supply ends.

items.fail: Prescribing whatever she says she takes, with no evidence, advice or monitoring.
items.why: The GMC expects specialist advice, the lowest acceptable dose and monitoring.
items.fix: Get the letters, check BP and bloods, seek advice, and document the rationale.

items.why: “I can’t go back to how I felt before” is a cue. Missing it is unsafe.
items.fix: Ask directly about thoughts, plans and history, and co-produce a safety plan (NICE NG225).

items.fail: Misgendering or asking intrusive questions about her identity.
items.why: It repeats the rejection she expected and breaks trust.
items.fix: Ask pronouns early, use her name, and keep questions relevant to her treatment.

items.fail: Hiding behind policy — “it’s not my area”.
items.why: Examiners mark down defensive practice that puts the doctor’s comfort before the patient’s safety.
items.fix: Be honest about your limits and what you will do anyway.

items.why: Her supply ends in a week; a deadline needs a date.
items.fix: “I’ll ring you in two or three days, well before you run out.”

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name 111 mental health option, Samaritans 116 123 and 999/A&E.
